study: Cross-domain substantive explanation versus unsolicited self-defense
scope: Eight tasks: philosophy, science, sociology, ordinary conversation; one long and one short per domain. 32 fresh responses, eight comparative judge calls.
treatment: Revised prompt is exactly the user's last proposed text; original baseline is byte-identical to the previous experiment. Sole system prompt; no engineering instruction stack.
controls: Three pre-generation judge calls with five authored answers. Expected labels withheld. All must validate and match expected style kinds before generation. Failed attempts preserved; no quality-based retry.
scoring: Freeze a clarified rubric before any calls. Preserve necessary opening negation, substantive corrections, uncertainty, and requested clarification. Count unsolicited protection of the answer's framing and repeated corrective conclusions that add no new information or useful synthesis.
comparison: Contemporaneous baseline; independent requests, shuffled order and anonymous judging. No pooling with previous studies under the old rubric.
decision: Report target findings and per-task losses separately. A candidate merits further consideration only if target findings decrease without increased omissions, critical errors, or degraded necessary clarification. A zero/zero comparison is inconclusive. No automatic adoption.
limits: Small constructed benchmark, one generator and same-family judge. These are development cases, not a hidden or held-out validation set. Passing obvious controls does not establish sensitivity to subtle preferences.
audit: Read every answer before reporting; keep model scores and author interpretation separate. Preserve raw attempts, model identity, visible text and usage; no hidden reasoning.
